1111.label: Bond formation or cleavage
why: One principal bond formed or broken
1111.boundary: For SN1 ionization, O1 follows the project convention for polar electron-pair bookkeeping; it does not claim a new donor–acceptor bond forms during departure. Alkene protonation follows the same inherited convention; inspect the mechanism for the accompanying π-bond change.

1122.label: Polar bond replacement
why: Occupied orbital donates into an acceptor orbital
One bond is replaced by another
Approach and departure are coupled in one event
1122.boundary: SN2 and direct proton transfer can share this code; the code does not distinguish a carbon from a hydrogen reaction center.

2211.label: Radical bond formation
why: Approach at the reaction center dominates
2211.boundary: Radical addition can convert a π bond into a σ bond; radical recombination can ultimately yield a closed-shell product.

1333.label: Concerted pericyclic reorganization
1333.boundary: Concerted does not mean synchronous. This code cannot distinguish cycloaddition, electrocyclization, and σ migration, so retain the reaction name.

1113.label: Carbonyl addition / elimination
why: n or σ donation into π*; reverse process restores the carbonyl
Nucleophilic bond formation or leaving-group cleavage dominates
The carbonyl center changes between planar and tetrahedral geometry
1113.boundary: This is an early candidate assignment, not a fixed v0.1 code. R3 is another possible boundary when π-bond-order change is emphasized.

1133.label: Polar multiple-bond reorganization
why: Donor–acceptor interaction between base and substrate
C–H, C–X, and C=C bonding changes are coupled
Several centers adjust together or form a planar π system
1133.boundary: A project candidate used for E2 and the alkene-forming E1 event. Concerted E2 chemistry is not automatically a pericyclic O3 reaction.

2222.label: Radical atom transfer
why: Singly occupied orbital interacts with a σ bond
An atom transfers between reaction centers
2222.boundary: A project candidate for H- or halogen-atom transfer; this is not a quantum-chemically validated classification.
